content.question: Under the shared responsibility model, which of these is ALWAYS the cloud provider's responsibility, regardless of service type?

options.B: The accounts and identities in your environment
options.C: Operating system patching
options.D: The devices allowed to connect to your cloud

content.explanation: The provider always owns the physical datacenter, physical network, physical hosts, and infrastructure. Why not the others: B — Always the customer's responsibility. · C — Depends on the service type: yours in IaaS, the provider's in PaaS/SaaS. · D — Always the customer's responsibility, in every service type.

content.question: Which of these is ALWAYS the customer's responsibility, regardless of service type?

options.A: The operating system on your servers
options.C: The information and data stored in the cloud
options.D: The physical hosts that run your workloads

content.explanation: Data, connecting devices, and accounts/identities always stay with the customer — even in SaaS. Why not the others: A — Depends on the service type (yours in IaaS only). · B — Depends on the service type. · D — Always the provider's responsibility.

content.question: Which cloud SERVICE TYPE places the most responsibility on the customer?

options.C: Hybrid cloud (mixing public and private)
options.D: Platform as a service (PaaS)

content.explanation: IaaS leaves the OS, network configuration, and most of the stack to you; the provider handles only physical security, power, and connectivity. Why not the others: A — SaaS places the least responsibility on the customer. · C — Hybrid is a deployment model (where resources run), not a service type — a classic distractor. · D — PaaS sits in the middle and splits responsibility more evenly.

content.question: What is the key difference between a public cloud and a private cloud?

options.A: Public cloud is open to any buyer; private cloud serves a single entity
options.B: A private cloud requires no capital expenditure to scale up
options.C: A public cloud gives you complete control over resources and security
options.D: A private cloud must be hosted in your own on-site datacenter

content.explanation: General public availability is the defining difference. A private cloud is dedicated to one organization. Why not the others: B — Backwards — private cloud requires buying hardware; 'no CapEx to scale' is a public-cloud trait. · C — That's a private-cloud trait; in public cloud you don't have complete control. · D — Wrong — a private cloud can be off-site, even run by a third party.

content.question: Which cloud model lets you decide where each application runs and keep control of security, compliance, or legal requirements while still using public cloud resources?

options.C: Multicloud
options.D: Private cloud

content.explanation: Hybrid combines public and private clouds in an interconnected environment and is described as the most flexible model — you choose where workloads run. Why not the others: A — You don't have complete control over resources and security in public cloud alone. · C — Multicloud means two or more PUBLIC providers; it doesn't imply a private component. · D — Gives control but doesn't by itself use public cloud resources.

content.question: Which scenario describes a multicloud environment?

options.A: Hosting a private cloud in a third party's dedicated datacenter
options.B: Combining a private cloud and one public cloud in a single interconnected environment
options.C: Running several subscriptions inside a single Azure account
options.D: Using two or more public cloud providers and managing resources and security in each

content.explanation: Multicloud = multiple public cloud providers, whether to use different features or mid-migration between providers. Why not the others: A — That's still a private cloud. · B — That's hybrid cloud. · C — Still one provider — not multicloud.

content.question: Which Azure offering helps you manage environments that are Azure-only, in your own private datacenter, hybrid, or spread across multiple cloud providers?

options.C: Azure Arc
options.D: Azure Migrate

content.explanation: Azure Arc is a set of technologies for managing cloud environments across public, private, hybrid, and multicloud. Why not the others: A — Hosts DNS domains; unrelated to managing hybrid or multicloud resources. · B — Runs your VMware workloads in Azure; it isn't a cross-environment management layer. · D — A migration hub for moving on-premises workloads into Azure, not ongoing cross-cloud management.

content.question: Cloud computing is classified as which type of expense, and why?

options.A: Capital expenditure (CapEx), because you rent compute and storage
options.B: Operational expenditure (OpEx), because you pay for services as you consume them
options.C: Operational expenditure (OpEx), because you buy hardware ahead of expected demand
options.D: Capital expenditure (CapEx), because the provider buys hardware up front

content.explanation: Pay-as-you-consume spending over time is OpEx. CapEx is up-front spending on physical infrastructure. Why not the others: A — Renting/consuming services is OpEx, not CapEx. · C — Right category, wrong reason — buying hardware ahead of demand is CapEx thinking. · D — The provider's hardware purchase isn't your expense category.

content.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of the consumption-based model?

options.A: The ability to release resources when demand decreases
options.B: No upfront costs for hardware or datacenter infrastructure
options.C: The ability to add resources when demand increases
options.D: A guaranteed fixed monthly bill regardless of how much you use

content.explanation: Consumption-based pricing means your bill tracks usage — it varies. That's the opposite of a fixed bill. Why not the others: A — This IS a listed benefit. · B — This IS a listed benefit. · C — This IS a listed benefit.

content.question: True or false? If you deploy a VM and install SQL Server on it yourself, the cloud provider is responsible for patching the database.
content.explanation: When you install the database yourself on IaaS, patches and updates are yours. With a managed cloud SQL database, the provider maintains the database itself.

content.question: True or false? In a private cloud, hardware must be purchased for startup and maintenance.
content.explanation: Listed in the comparison table — private cloud brings control but also hardware costs and maintenance.

content.question: True or false? In a traditional datacenter, overestimating capacity leads to degraded application performance.
content.explanation: Swapped on purpose: OVERestimating means overspending on idle infrastructure; UNDERestimating causes degraded performance.

content.question: True or false? In a public cloud, you don't have complete control over resources and security.
content.explanation: This is one of the listed trade-offs of public cloud in the module's comparison table.

content.question: True or false? In PaaS and SaaS, identity and access is shared: you manage users, roles, and policies while the provider runs the authentication platform.
content.explanation: The module gives exactly this example — e.g., the provider runs Microsoft Entra ID while you manage your own users and policies.

content.question: True or false? A private cloud must be hosted in your organization's own on-site datacenter.
content.explanation: A private cloud can be hosted on-site, in a dedicated off-site datacenter, or even by a third party. What makes it private is that it's used by a single entity.

content.question: Scenario: A company runs its private cloud on VMware and wants to move those workloads into Azure with minimal re-platforming, keeping VMware integration. Which option fits best?

options.A: Add a second public cloud provider to create a multicloud setup
options.C: Rebuild every workload as a SaaS application
options.D: Azure VMware Solution

content.explanation: Azure VMware Solution is built for exactly this: run VMware workloads in Azure with seamless integration and scalability. Why not the others: A — Doesn't move the VMware workloads into Azure at all. · B — Arc manages resources wherever they run; it doesn't host your VMware workloads in Azure. · C — Massive re-platforming — the opposite of the requirement.

content.question: Scenario: A retailer's private cloud handles normal load well, but holiday traffic creates temporary surges. Regulations require customer payment data to stay on the company's private infrastructure. Which approach fits best?

options.A: Stay private-only and buy enough hardware to cover the holiday peak
options.B: Move everything to the public cloud
options.C: Hybrid cloud: keep payment data private, burst to public for surges
options.D: Adopt a multicloud design across two public providers

content.explanation: Hybrid lets a private cloud burst into public cloud for temporary demand while you choose which services stay private — meeting both requirements. Why not the others: A — Works, but leaves expensive capacity idle most of the year (classic overestimate problem). · B — Breaks the requirement that payment data stays on private infrastructure. · D — Multicloud is public-only; it doesn't keep payment data on private infrastructure.

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: Which action is an example of vertical scaling?

options.A: Using a load balancer to spread traffic across servers
options.B: Adding more virtual machines when demand spikes
options.C: Deploying a copy of the app in another region for failover
options.D: Adding more CPUs or RAM to an existing virtual machine

content.explanation: Vertical scaling changes the capability of a resource (scale up/down). Horizontal scaling changes the number of resources (scale out/in). Why not the others: A — Load balancing supports performance predictability; it isn't vertical scaling. · B — That's horizontal scaling (scaling out). · C — That's a reliability design choice, not scaling.

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: What does it mean to 'scale in'?

options.A: Choosing a service with a lower SLA tier
options.B: Reducing the number of instances, such as removing VMs
options.C: Reducing the CPU or RAM of an existing VM
options.D: Consolidating all resources into a single region

content.explanation: Scale in is the horizontal direction (fewer instances). Scale down is vertical (smaller CPU/RAM). Why not the others: A — Not scaling; SLAs are availability guarantees. · C — That's scaling down (vertical). · D — Not a scaling operation.

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: Where are Azure's uptime guarantees for each service defined?

options.C: In the Azure Well-Architected Framework
options.D: In resource tags

content.explanation: Azure uptime guarantees vary by service and are part of the SLAs — key to high availability planning. Why not the others: A — That estimates cost, not uptime. · C — That's design guidance, not a contractual uptime guarantee. · D — Tags are metadata you add; they don't define Azure's guarantees.

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: Which definition describes RELIABILITY in the cloud?

options.A: Recovering from failures and continuing to function
options.C: Adjusting resources to meet changing demand
options.D: Maximizing uptime regardless of disruptions, backed by SLAs

content.explanation: Reliability = recover and keep functioning (a pillar of the Well-Architected Framework). High availability = maximize uptime regardless of disruptions. Close, but tested separately. Why not the others: B — That's cost predictability. · C — That's scalability. · D — That's high availability — the near-miss distractor.

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: Which of these supports PERFORMANCE predictability (rather than cost predictability)?

options.A: Analyzing spending trends to plan future deployments
options.B: Tracking resource use and spend in real time
options.C: Autoscaling and load balancing
options.D: Estimating spend with the Azure Pricing Calculator

content.explanation: Autoscaling, load balancing, and high availability are the module's examples of performance predictability. Why not the others: A — Cost predictability. · B — Cost predictability. · D — Cost predictability.

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: Which is an example of management IN the cloud (how you manage), rather than management OF the cloud?

options.A: Deploying resources from a preconfigured template
options.B: Receiving automatic alerts based on configured metrics
options.C: Automatically scaling resources based on need
options.D: Managing resources through PowerShell

content.explanation: Management IN the cloud = the tools you use: web portal, CLI, APIs, PowerShell. Management OF the cloud = what the cloud does for your resources: autoscale, templates, health monitoring, alerts. Why not the others: A — Management OF the cloud. · B — Management OF the cloud. · C — Management OF the cloud.

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: Which type of attack are cloud providers described as typically well suited to handle, making your network more robust?

options.A: Misuse of admin accounts by your own staff
options.B: SQL injection flaws in your custom application code
options.C: Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks
options.D: Phishing attacks against your users' passwords

content.explanation: The module calls out DDoS specifically — provider scale lets them absorb and filter large attacks. Why not the others: A — Managing your accounts and access is always your responsibility. · B — Your own app code is your responsibility. · D — Protecting your users' credentials is your identity responsibility.

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: Which practice supports BOTH sustainability and cost efficiency?

options.A: Overprovisioning VMs so you never have to scale
options.B: Automatically shutting down a dev environment outside business hours
options.C: Keeping unused resources allocated in case they're needed later
options.D: Always choosing the largest VM size for extra headroom

content.explanation: Turning off or deallocating unused resources reduces unnecessary consumption — the module's own example. Why not the others: A — Overprovisioning is waste — the opposite of right-sizing. · C — Idle resources waste energy and money. · D — Same problem — avoid overprovisioning.

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: True or false? Cloud-based auditing can flag resources that are out of compliance with your baseline and suggest mitigations.
content.explanation: Called out directly in the security and governance unit.

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: True or false? After a regional disaster in Azure, you always have to move workloads to another region manually.
content.explanation: You can design apps to fail over automatically, and in some cases Azure shifts to another region for you with no action needed.

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: True or false? Vertical scaling means adding or removing resources, such as VMs or containers.
content.explanation: That's horizontal scaling. Vertical scaling changes a resource's capabilities (CPU/RAM).

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: True or false? Because the cloud is consumption-based, reducing resources when demand drops also reduces your costs.
content.explanation: Scalability means you aren't overpaying — scale down/in and you pay less.

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: True or false? The Azure Pricing Calculator is a tool for performance predictability.
content.explanation: The Pricing Calculator supports COST predictability by estimating spend.

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: True or false? Horizontal scaling can be done automatically or manually.
content.explanation: Resources can be scaled out or in either automatically or manually.

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: Scenario: An online store sees 5x traffic for a few hours on flash-sale days and normal traffic otherwise. Leadership wants to handle the spikes without paying for idle capacity the rest of the time. What should the team do?

options.A: Autoscale out during spikes, then scale back in
options.B: Use the Pricing Calculator to forecast the spike
options.C: Deploy a second copy in another region for reliability
options.D: Permanently scale every VM up to the largest available size

content.explanation: Horizontal autoscaling matches capacity to demand, and the consumption model means you stop paying when you scale in. Why not the others: B — Forecasting cost doesn't add capacity during the spike. · C — Improves reliability, but doesn't address demand or cost. · D — Pays for peak capacity 24/7 — exactly what they want to avoid.

topic: Describe the benefits of using cloud services

content.question: Scenario: An operations team wants to (1) deploy consistent resources without manual configuration, (2) get notified automatically when performance metrics cross thresholds, and (3) automate recurring tasks with scripts. Which combination fits?

options.A: Templates for deployment, metric-based alerts, and CLI or PowerShell scripts
options.B: The Pricing Calculator, tags, and budgets
options.C: Manual portal configuration for every resource, plus daily dashboard checks
options.D: Region pairs, SLAs, and DDoS protection

content.explanation: This combines management OF the cloud (templates, alerts) with management IN the cloud (CLI/PowerShell), matching the module's ops example. Why not the others: B — These are cost-management tools. · C — Manual and reactive — fails requirements 1 and 2. · D — These address reliability and security, not deployment or automation.

content.question: In an IaaS model, what is the cloud provider responsible for?

options.A: Database and storage configuration and tuning
options.B: Hardware, physical security, and internet connectivity
options.C: Operating system installation, configuration, and maintenance
options.D: Network configuration within your environment

content.explanation: In IaaS the provider keeps the hardware, internet connectivity, and physical security; you handle everything else. Why not the others: A — Yours in IaaS. · C — Yours in IaaS. · D — Yours in IaaS.

content.question: In which model do you NOT have to worry about OS or database licensing and patching, but you still manage your own application code and data?

options.C: Platform as a service (PaaS)
options.D: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS)

content.explanation: PaaS providers maintain the OS, middleware, development tools, and runtimes; you focus on your code, data, and access controls. Why not the others: A — On-premises, you're responsible for everything. · B — In SaaS you don't write or manage the application code. · D — In IaaS you patch and license the OS yourself.

content.question: Which statement correctly compares the service types?

options.A: IaaS is the most flexible; SaaS is the easiest to get up and running
options.B: IaaS is the least flexible but needs the least expertise
options.C: SaaS is the most flexible; IaaS is the easiest to get running
options.D: PaaS is both the most flexible and the easiest model to get up and running

content.explanation: IaaS gives maximum control and flexibility. SaaS is the least flexible but needs the least technical expertise. Why not the others: B — IaaS is the most flexible and needs the most expertise. · C — Reversed. · D — PaaS is the middle ground on both.

content.question: A team wants to move existing on-premises workloads to the cloud by recreating a similar environment, with minimal changes. Which service type fits?

options.B: None — lift-and-shift requires redesigning the app first
options.C: IaaS
options.D: PaaS

content.explanation: Lift-and-shift migration is a named IaaS scenario: set up cloud resources similar to your datacenter and move workloads over. Why not the others: A — SaaS replaces the app with a finished product; it doesn't host your existing workloads. · B — The point of lift-and-shift is minimal redesign. · D — PaaS usually requires adapting the app to the managed platform.

content.question: Which is a typical SaaS example?

options.A: Renting virtual machines to host a custom app
options.B: Provider-supplied tools to analyze and mine your own data
options.C: A hosted email and messaging application
options.D: A managed framework developers build custom cloud apps on

content.explanation: Email, messaging, productivity, and finance/expense apps are the module's SaaS examples. Why not the others: A — IaaS. · B — Analytics/BI is listed as a PaaS scenario — a common trap. · D — PaaS (development framework scenario).

content.question: In SaaS, what does the customer still primarily manage?

options.A: Operating system updates and security fixes
options.B: The runtime, middleware, and app servers
options.C: Application patches and feature updates
options.D: Their data, identities and access, and devices

content.explanation: The SaaS provider runs almost the whole stack, but your data, identities, and devices stay with you. Why not the others: A — Provider-managed in SaaS. · B — Provider-managed in SaaS (and PaaS). · C — The SaaS provider handles application maintenance.

content.question: Which of these is NOT one of the common PaaS scenarios described in the module?

options.B: A development framework to build or customize cloud apps
options.C: Building apps with built-in scalability and high availability
options.D: Lift-and-shift migration of existing servers

content.explanation: Lift-and-shift is an IaaS scenario. PaaS scenarios are development frameworks and analytics/business intelligence. Why not the others: A — This IS a PaaS scenario. · B — This IS a PaaS scenario. · C — This is part of the PaaS development framework scenario.

content.question: True or false? In PaaS, the customer is responsible for patching the operating system.
content.explanation: The PaaS provider maintains operating systems, middleware, and runtimes.

content.question: True or false? Moving from IaaS to SaaS increases the operational responsibility on the customer.
content.explanation: The opposite — responsibility shifts toward the provider as you move IaaS → PaaS → SaaS.

content.question: True or false? SaaS requires the least technical knowledge to fully use.
content.explanation: SaaS is the easiest model to get running and needs the least expertise.

content.question: True or false? With IaaS, you're essentially renting hardware in a cloud datacenter, and what you do with it is up to you.
content.explanation: Nearly word-for-word the module's description of IaaS.

content.question: True or false? In SaaS, the customer is no longer responsible for their data because the provider manages the application.
content.explanation: Data is ALWAYS the customer's responsibility, in every service type.

content.question: True or false? PaaS includes cloud features like scalability and high availability, reducing how much code developers must write.
content.explanation: Part of the development framework scenario for PaaS.

content.question: Scenario: A startup's developers want to build a custom web API. They don't want to manage OS patches or middleware, and they want scaling and high availability built in. Which model fits best?

options.C: An on-premises private cloud
options.D: SaaS

content.explanation: PaaS gives a managed platform for custom code, with scalability and HA included and no OS/middleware maintenance. Why not the others: B — They'd have to manage the OS and patching themselves. · C — Maximum management overhead — the opposite of the goal. · D — SaaS is a finished application; you can't build your own API on it.

content.question: Scenario: A company wants to (1) replace its on-premises email server with a hosted email service, and (2) move a legacy app that needs a custom OS configuration to the cloud as-is. Which pairing fits best?

options.A: SaaS for email; PaaS for the legacy app
options.B: SaaS for email; IaaS for the legacy app
options.C: IaaS for both
options.D: PaaS for email; SaaS for the legacy app

content.explanation: Email is a textbook SaaS case. A legacy app needing custom OS settings needs IaaS control (lift-and-shift). Why not the others: A — PaaS doesn't give you control over the OS configuration. · C — Running your own email servers on VMs keeps all the maintenance — SaaS is the better fit. · D — SaaS can't host your custom legacy app.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: What is an Azure availability zone?

options.A: An isolated instance of Azure used for government or legal compliance needs
options.B: A pair of regions in the same geography at least 300 miles apart
options.C: A logical container for resources that share the same lifecycle
options.D: Physically separate datacenters within one region, each with independent power and cooling

content.explanation: Availability zones are isolation boundaries inside one region: if one zone goes down, the others keep working. Why not the others: A — That's a sovereign region. · B — That's a region pair. · C — That's a resource group.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: How many availability zones are present, at minimum, in every availability zone-enabled region?

options.C: Three
options.D: Four

content.explanation: A minimum of three separate zones ensures resiliency. Note: not every region supports zones. Why not the others: A — Six is the management group nesting depth — a different number. · B — Too few — the minimum is three. · D — More than the guaranteed minimum.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: Which of these is a ZONE-REDUNDANT service, where the platform replicates across zones automatically?

options.B: Virtual machines deployed to a zone
options.C: Public IP addresses
options.D: Azure SQL Database

content.explanation: Zone-redundant services (the module's examples are zone-redundant storage and SQL Database) replicate across zones for you. Zonal services are pinned to one zone you choose. Why not the others: A — Zonal. · B — Zonal — you pin a VM to a specific zone. · C — Listed as zonal in the module.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: Most Azure regions are paired with another region in the same geography that is at least how far away?

options.C: 1,000 miles
options.D: 100 miles

content.explanation: Region pairs sit at least 300 miles apart so a single regional disaster is unlikely to hit both. Why not the others: B — Not the stated minimum. · C — Not the stated minimum. · D — Too close.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: Which region is paired in only ONE direction, with a secondary region outside its own geography?

options.C: West US (paired with East US)
options.D: Southeast Asia (paired with East Asia)

content.explanation: Brazil South's secondary is South Central US, but South Central US's secondary is NOT Brazil South. It's the classic one-direction exception. Why not the others: A — Italy North has no traditional pair; it relies on availability zones and geo-redundant storage instead. · C — A standard two-way pair. · D — A standard two-way pair in the same geography.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: Which service is global and does NOT require you to choose a region?

options.C: Microsoft Entra ID
options.D: Azure Virtual Network

content.explanation: Microsoft Entra ID, Azure Traffic Manager, and Azure DNS are named as global services that don't need a region selection. Why not the others: A — VMs are deployed into a region you choose. · B — You choose a primary region for a storage account. · D — Virtual networks are regional resources.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: How are the Azure China sovereign regions (such as China East and China North) operated?

options.A: Directly by Microsoft as one part of the single, global Azure public instance
options.B: Via a 21Vianet partnership; Microsoft doesn't directly run the datacenters
options.C: By screened U.S. personnel with extra compliance certifications
options.D: As standard public regions paired with US regions

content.explanation: This is the distinguishing fact for the China sovereign regions. Why not the others: A — Sovereign regions are isolated, and Microsoft doesn't directly maintain the China datacenters. · C — That describes US government regions (US DoD Central, US Gov Virginia). · D — They're isolated from the main instance of Azure.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: Which statement about resource groups is TRUE?

options.A: A resource can belong to several resource groups at once
options.B: Resource groups can be nested inside other resource groups
options.C: A resource group can be renamed after it's created
options.D: Deleting a resource group deletes every resource inside it

content.explanation: Actions on a resource group apply to everything in it — including deletion. That's why grouping by lifecycle is useful. Why not the others: A — Every resource belongs to exactly one resource group at a time. · B — Resource groups can't be nested. · C — Resource groups can't be renamed.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: Which two types of boundaries does an Azure subscription provide?

options.A: A billing boundary and an access control boundary
options.B: A geographic boundary and a data residency boundary
options.C: A network boundary and a DNS boundary
options.D: A fault boundary and an update boundary

content.explanation: Each subscription gets separate billing reports/invoices, and access-management policies are applied at the subscription level. Why not the others: B — Those relate to regions and geographies. · C — Those relate to virtual networks and DNS zones. · D — Fault and update domains belong to VM availability sets.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: How many levels deep can management groups be nested (not counting the root level or the subscription level)?

options.C: Six
options.D: Three

content.explanation: Six levels of depth. Don't confuse it with 10,000, the maximum number of management groups in a single directory. Why not the others: A — Not the limit. · B — That's the max NUMBER of management groups per directory, not nesting depth. · D — Too few.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: What is the correct hierarchy, from top to bottom?

options.A: Management groups → subscriptions → resource groups → resources
options.B: Subscriptions → management groups → resource groups → resources
options.C: Management groups → resource groups → subscriptions → resources
options.D: Resource groups → subscriptions → management groups → resources

content.explanation: Resources live in resource groups, resource groups in subscriptions, subscriptions under management groups (all under the Tenant Root Group). Why not the others: B — Management groups sit ABOVE subscriptions. · C — Resource groups sit inside subscriptions. · D — Upside down.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: True or false? An Azure account can have only one subscription.
content.explanation: An account can have multiple subscriptions; only one is required.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: True or false? Each management group and each subscription can have only one parent.
content.explanation: Listed as an important fact about management groups.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: True or false? All Azure services automatically replicate data and fail over to the paired region.
content.explanation: Not all services do. In those cases, the customer must configure recovery and replication.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: True or false? Every Azure region supports availability zones.
content.explanation: Not all regions currently support availability zones.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: True or false? Every Microsoft Entra tenant has a single top-level Tenant Root Group.
content.explanation: All other management groups and subscriptions fold up to it, so you can apply governance globally.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: True or false? Planned Azure updates are rolled out to paired regions one region at a time.
content.explanation: This minimizes downtime and the risk of an application outage.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: True or false? A policy applied at a management group can be overridden by the owner of a subscription beneath it.
content.explanation: Inherited management-group policies can't be overridden by the resource or subscription owner — that's what strengthens governance.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: Scenario: An app must keep running if a single datacenter in its region fails. Data must stay in the same region, and the team wants the simplest design that meets this goal. What should they do?

options.A: Place all VMs in a single availability zone
options.B: Split the resources across several resource groups in the region
options.C: Move the workload to a sovereign region
options.D: Spread resources across availability zones in the region

content.explanation: Availability zones are physically separate datacenters in one region, so they protect against a datacenter failure without leaving the region. Why not the others: A — One zone failing would take everything down. · B — Resource groups are logical containers, not physical isolation. · C — Sovereign regions are about compliance isolation, not datacenter resilience.

topic: Describe the core architectural components of Azure

content.question: Scenario: The IT department has eight subscriptions. You must (1) restrict VM deployments to approved regions in all of them and (2) give the security team Reader access to all of them, with the least ongoing effort. What should you do?

options.A: Create a separate Azure account for the IT department
options.B: Group them under an IT management group; assign policy and Reader role there
options.C: Merge all of the IT resources into one resource group in a single subscription
options.D: Assign the policy and role separately on every resource group

content.explanation: Policy and RBAC assignments at a management group inherit to every subscription, resource group, and resource beneath it. Why not the others: A — A new account doesn't apply governance across the existing subscriptions. · C — Disruptive and unnecessary — management groups exist for this. · D — Works, but it's high effort and new resource groups can be missed.

content.question: In the VM size name Standard_D2s_v5, what does the 's' indicate?

options.A: It belongs to the storage-optimized family
options.C: The size supports Premium SSD storage
options.D: It's a small size within the D family

content.explanation: Decode: D = family (general purpose), 2 = vCPUs, s = Premium SSD support, v5 = hardware generation. Why not the others: A — Storage-optimized is the L-series. · B — Spot isn't encoded in the size name. · D — The number (2) indicates size via vCPU count.

content.question: Which VM family is designed for GPU workloads such as AI training and graphics?

options.C: B-series
options.D: F-series

content.explanation: N-series = GPU enabled. Memorize the family letters: B burstable, D general purpose, E memory, F compute, M large memory, L storage, N GPU. Why not the others: A — Memory optimized. · C — Burstable, cost-efficient dev/test. · D — Compute optimized (CPU-intensive).

content.question: Which feature creates and manages a group of identical, load-balanced VMs that can automatically add or remove instances as demand changes?

options.C: Availability sets
options.D: Availability zones

content.explanation: Scale sets centralize configuration and autoscale based on demand or schedules, integrated with load balancing. Why not the others: A — Desktop and app virtualization for users. · C — These improve resiliency via update and fault domains; they don't autoscale. · D — Physical datacenter isolation within a region, not a VM scaling feature.

content.question: How do availability sets group VMs?

options.C: By availability zone and datacenter
options.D: By update domain and fault domain

content.explanation: Update domain = VMs that can reboot together during planned maintenance. Fault domain = VMs sharing a power/network failure point. Why not the others: A — Those are management/organization concepts. · B — Those are geography concepts. · C — That's zone-based design, which availability sets aren't.

content.question: Which Azure container service is an ORCHESTRATION service that manages the lifecycle of a fleet of containers?

options.C: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
options.D: Azure Container Apps

content.explanation: AKS is the orchestration option. ACI is the fastest/simplest way to run a container; Container Apps add built-in scaling without you managing orchestration. Why not the others: A — Simplest way to run a single container; no orchestration. · B — Web/API hosting platform, not container orchestration. · D — PaaS with built-in load balancing and scaling, but not the orchestration answer.

content.question: Which container option is PaaS AND includes built-in load balancing and scaling?

options.C: Virtual Machine Scale Sets
options.D: Azure Container Apps

content.explanation: Container Apps are similar to Container Instances but add built-in load balancing and scaling. Why not the others: A — PaaS and simple, but the module doesn't credit it with built-in scaling and load balancing. · B — An orchestration service; you take on more management. · C — Scale VMs, not containers as a PaaS service.

content.question: How are you typically charged for Azure Functions in the serverless model?

options.A: A flat monthly fee per function app
options.B: Only for the CPU time used while the function runs
options.C: For the VM hours your app consumes, whether or not events occur
options.D: Per container instance hour

content.explanation: Functions are woken by events and automatically deallocated when finished — you pay only while code executes. Why not the others: A — Not the serverless model. · C — That's VM billing — Functions don't need running VMs. · D — Functions don't require you to maintain containers.

content.question: Which App Service feature runs a program or script in the same context as a web app, often for background tasks?

options.C: Mobile apps
options.D: API apps

content.explanation: WebJobs run programs (.exe, Java, PHP, Python, Node.js) or scripts (.cmd, .bat, PowerShell, Bash), scheduled or triggered. Why not the others: B — A separate serverless service, not an App Service app type. · C — A back end for iOS/Android apps. · D — Host REST APIs with Swagger support.

content.question: A team needs to build, train, and manage its own CUSTOM machine learning model. Which service fits?

options.C: Azure IoT Hub
options.D: Azure AI services

content.explanation: Azure Machine Learning = custom model development and lifecycle. Azure AI services = prebuilt AI through APIs. Why not the others: B — A SaaS IoT platform. · C — Device-to-cloud messaging. · D — Prebuilt capabilities (language, speech, vision) — no custom training required.

content.question: Which service provides secure, bi-directional communication between cloud services and IoT devices?

options.C: Azure IoT Edge
options.D: Azure IoT Hub

content.explanation: IoT Hub is the messaging backbone. IoT Central is a SaaS IoT platform; IoT Edge runs workloads near the devices. Why not the others: A — Prebuilt AI APIs, not device communication. · B — Simplified SaaS IoT platform for solution builders. · C — Extends cloud workloads to edge devices.

content.question: True or false? Agentic AI is its own separate Azure compute service category.
content.explanation: The module says to treat agentic AI as an application pattern built from Azure AI capabilities, not a separate compute category.

content.question: True or false? Azure Container Instances is a platform as a service (PaaS) offering.
content.explanation: You upload containers and the service runs them for you.

content.question: True or false? With containers, you manage the operating system of each container just as you would for a VM.
content.explanation: Unlike VMs, you don't manage the OS for a container — that's part of why they're lightweight.

content.question: True or false? Azure VMs are IaaS, so you still manage patching and configuration inside the VM.
content.explanation: VMs remove hardware maintenance, not OS maintenance.

content.question: True or false? Azure Functions are stateless by default.
content.explanation: Stateless is the default; stateful functions are Durable Functions, where the runtime passes context to track prior activity.

content.question: True or false? Azure App Service supports only Windows as the host operating system.
content.explanation: App Service supports both Windows and Linux.

content.question: True or false? Availability sets add cost on top of the VMs you place in them.
content.explanation: Availability sets themselves don't add cost; you pay for the VM instances.

content.question: True or false? Azure Virtual Desktop supports both single-session and multi-session Windows experiences.
content.explanation: Listed as a key point of Azure Virtual Desktop.

content.question: Scenario: A website is split into a front end, a back end, and a storage component. The back end regularly hits capacity while the others are idle. The team wants to scale and update each part independently, without managing operating systems, and will run a large fleet of containers that needs lifecycle management. What fits best?

options.A: Deliver the app through an Azure Virtual Desktop host pool
options.B: Host everything on one large VM and scale it up vertically when it's needed
options.C: Containerize each component as a microservice and run the fleet on AKS
options.D: Put identical VMs in an availability set

content.explanation: Containers suit microservice architectures (scale the back end alone), and AKS manages the lifecycle of a container fleet. Why not the others: A — AVD delivers desktops to users, not web app components. · B — Scales everything together, and you manage the OS. · D — Adds resiliency, but doesn't let each component scale independently.

content.question: Scenario: Whenever a user uploads an image to storage, a thumbnail must be generated, which takes under two seconds. Uploads are unpredictable and there are often none for hours. The goal is to pay as little as possible while idle. What should you use?

options.A: Azure Functions triggered by the upload event
options.B: An AKS cluster with a dedicated node pool
options.C: An always-on App Service web app
options.D: A Virtual Machine Scale Set with two instances minimum

content.explanation: Event-driven, short-running, variable-demand work is the textbook Functions case, and you pay only while the code runs. Why not the others: B — Overkill, and nodes cost money while idle. · C — Pays for a running plan around the clock. · D — Those instances bill even when no uploads occur.

content.question: What is a private endpoint?

options.A: A DNS alias record that points to an Azure resource
options.B: An endpoint with a public IP address that can be reached from anywhere in the world
options.C: An endpoint in a virtual network, using a private IP from its address space
options.D: A VPN gateway deployed in a dedicated gateway subnet

content.explanation: Private endpoints live inside a VNet with a private IP. Public endpoints have a public IP reachable from anywhere. Why not the others: A — That's an Azure DNS feature. · B — That's a public endpoint. · D — That's a VPN gateway, not an endpoint type.

content.question: Which describes a point-to-site VPN connection?

options.A: An on-premises VPN device links to the Azure VPN gateway
options.B: A single client computer opens an encrypted VPN to the virtual network
options.C: A dedicated private link to Azure that avoids the internet
options.D: Two virtual networks connecting directly over the Microsoft backbone network

content.explanation: Point-to-site = one device. Site-to-site = your on-premises VPN device to the Azure VPN gateway. Why not the others: A — That's site-to-site. · C — That's ExpressRoute. · D — That's virtual network peering.

content.question: How does traffic travel between two peered virtual networks?

options.A: Privately over the Microsoft backbone, never touching the internet
options.B: Only between VNets in the same region
options.C: Only through an ExpressRoute circuit
options.D: Encrypted over the public internet through VPN gateways

content.explanation: Peering traffic is private and stays on Microsoft's backbone — even when the VNets are in different regions. Why not the others: B — Peered VNets can be in separate regions. · C — Peering doesn't need ExpressRoute. · D — That's a VPN connection, not peering.

content.question: Which resource lets you allow or block traffic using inbound and outbound rules based on source/destination IP, port, and protocol?

options.C: Virtual network peering
options.D: Network security group (NSG)

content.explanation: NSGs hold multiple inbound/outbound security rules on exactly those factors. Why not the others: A — Controls where traffic is routed, not whether it's allowed. · B — Name resolution, not traffic filtering. · C — Connects VNets; it doesn't filter traffic.

content.question: How many VPN gateways can you deploy in a single virtual network?

options.C: As many as you need
options.D: Two — one active and one standby

content.explanation: Only one VPN gateway per VNet, but that one gateway can connect to multiple on-premises sites or other VNets. Why not the others: B — The gateway lives in one dedicated subnet; it's one per VNet. · C — The limit is one per VNet. · D — Active/standby is two INSTANCES behind one gateway resource, not two gateways.

content.question: You need point-to-site connections and coexistence with an ExpressRoute gateway. Which VPN gateway type is required?

options.C: Policy-based
options.D: Active/standby

content.explanation: Route-based is required for VNet-to-VNet, point-to-site, multisite, and ExpressRoute coexistence. It's also the preferred type for on-premises devices. Why not the others: B — That's a deployment option for resilience, not a VPN type. · C — Policy-based gateways use static IP lists and don't support these connection types. · D — That's a high-availability configuration, not a VPN type.

content.question: By default, how are VPN gateways deployed for high availability?

options.A: As two instances in active/active mode
options.B: As a single instance with no failover
options.C: As two instances in an active/standby configuration
options.D: As a zone-redundant gateway in every region

content.explanation: Even though you see one gateway resource, two instances run active/standby, and failover is automatic. Why not the others: A — Active/active is optional and uses BGP with a public IP per instance. · B — There's always a standby instance by default. · D — Zone-redundant requires specific SKUs and AZ-enabled regions.

content.question: What does ExpressRoute Global Reach let you do?

options.A: Reach Microsoft 365 and Dynamics 365 over a private ExpressRoute connection
options.B: Link your own on-premises sites to each other via their circuits
options.C: Fail over to an encrypted tunnel over the internet
options.D: Connect two virtual networks in different Azure regions

content.explanation: Example: an office in Asia and a datacenter in Europe exchange data over the Microsoft network instead of the internet. Why not the others: A — That's standard ExpressRoute connectivity to Microsoft cloud services. · C — That's using a VPN gateway as backup for ExpressRoute. · D — That's global VNet peering.

content.question: Even when you use ExpressRoute, which type of traffic is still sent over the public internet?

options.C: Traffic to Azure Storage
options.D: Traffic to Azure Virtual Machines

content.explanation: DNS queries, certificate revocation list checks, and Azure CDN requests still go over the public internet. Why not the others: A — Reachable over ExpressRoute. · C — Reachable over ExpressRoute. · D — Reachable over ExpressRoute.

content.question: Which of the following can Azure DNS NOT do?

options.A: Host DNS records for your domains on Azure name servers
options.B: Create alias records that point to Azure resources
options.C: Provide private DNS domains inside virtual networks
options.D: Buy or register a domain name

content.explanation: Azure DNS hosts and manages records. To buy a domain, use App Service domains or a third-party registrar. Why not the others: A — That's its core purpose. · B — Supported. · C — Supported.

content.question: True or false? Peered virtual networks can be in separate Azure regions.
content.explanation: Peering across regions lets you build a globally interconnected network.

content.question: True or false? Policy-based VPNs are preferred for on-premises devices because they handle topology changes better.
content.explanation: Route-based VPNs are preferred and are more resilient to topology changes such as new subnets.

content.question: True or false? ExpressRoute connections travel over the public internet but are encrypted end-to-end.
content.explanation: ExpressRoute connections don't go over the public internet at all. That's the point of a private circuit.

content.question: True or false? Azure DNS alias record sets automatically update when the underlying resource's IP address changes.
content.explanation: Alias records point to the service instance, so they track IP changes.

content.question: True or false? The IP range defined for a virtual network is routable on the internet.
content.explanation: The range exists only within the virtual network and isn't internet routable.

content.question: True or false? Azure VPN gateways authenticate with a preshared key, whether policy-based or route-based.
content.explanation: The module states the preshared key is used regardless of VPN type.

content.question: True or false? Site-to-site VPN connections are encrypted and travel over the internet.
content.explanation: A VPN is an encrypted tunnel over an untrusted network — usually the internet.

content.question: Scenario: A bank needs a private connection between its datacenter and Azure with predictable latency and high throughput, avoiding the public internet. It also wants a backup path in case the circuit itself has an outage. What should it deploy?

options.A: ExpressRoute alone, since its built-in redundancy makes any backup unnecessary
options.B: Virtual network peering from the datacenter to Azure
options.C: A point-to-site VPN connection from every server
options.D: ExpressRoute as the primary link, with a site-to-site VPN gateway as failover

content.explanation: ExpressRoute meets the private/predictable requirement; a VPN gateway over the internet is the documented failover path for circuit outages. Why not the others: A — Built-in redundancy doesn't protect against cable or location-wide outages. · B — Peering connects Azure VNets, not on-premises networks. · C — Internet-based and per-device — doesn't meet the private requirement.

content.question: Scenario: A web tier and a database tier are in separate subnets. Only the web subnet may reach the database on port 1433, and all outbound internet traffic must pass through a firewall appliance. What should you configure?

options.A: ExpressRoute with Global Reach enabled on the circuit
options.B: Private DNS zones plus virtual network peering between the web and DB tiers
options.C: NSG rules on the DB subnet plus user-defined routes to a firewall NVA
options.D: Public endpoints on both tiers with an alias record

content.explanation: NSGs filter by IP/port/protocol; user-defined routes steer traffic; a network virtual appliance performs the firewall function. Why not the others: A — That's on-premises connectivity, not subnet filtering. · B — Name resolution and VNet connectivity don't filter or force-route traffic. · D — Exposes the database publicly — the opposite of the goal.

content.question: Which storage account type supports ALL redundancy options (LRS, GRS, RA-GRS, ZRS, GZRS, RA-GZRS)?

options.C: Premium page blobs
options.D: Premium block blobs

content.explanation: Standard general-purpose v2 is recommended for most scenarios and supports every redundancy option. Premium types are limited to LRS/ZRS (page blobs: LRS only). Why not the others: B — LRS and ZRS only. · C — LRS only. · D — LRS and ZRS only.

content.question: Which rule applies to storage account names?

options.A: May include uppercase letters, numbers, and hyphens
options.B: Up to 63 characters, lowercase letters and numbers
options.C: 3–24 lowercase letters and numbers, globally unique in Azure
options.D: Unique within your subscription, and up to 24 characters long

content.explanation: The name forms part of a public endpoint URL, so it must be globally unique. Why not the others: A — Lowercase letters and numbers only. · B — Maximum is 24. · D — Must be unique across all of Azure.

content.question: What is the endpoint format for Azure Files?

options.C: https://<account>.table.core.windows.net
options.D: https://<account>.file.core.windows.net

content.explanation: Each service has its own subdomain: blob, dfs (Data Lake Gen2), file, queue, table. Why not the others: A — Blob Storage. · B — Data Lake Storage Gen2. · C — Table Storage.

content.question: How does locally redundant storage (LRS) replicate data?

options.A: Three times within a single datacenter in the primary region
options.B: Synchronously across three availability zones in the primary region
options.C: Three times locally, then asynchronously to a secondary region
options.D: Across zones in the primary region, then to a secondary region

content.explanation: LRS is the lowest-cost option and protects against rack/drive failures, but not a datacenter-level disaster. Why not the others: B — That's ZRS. · C — That's GRS. · D — That's GZRS.

content.question: How does geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) replicate data?

options.A: ZRS in both the primary and secondary regions
options.B: LRS in both the primary and secondary regions
options.C: ZRS in the primary region, then LRS in the secondary region
options.D: LRS in the primary region, then ZRS in the secondary

content.explanation: GZRS = ZRS primary + LRS secondary. GRS = LRS primary + LRS secondary. The secondary is always LRS. Why not the others: A — The secondary region is always LRS. · B — That's GRS. · D — Reversed.

content.question: What does choosing RA-GRS instead of GRS add?

options.A: Synchronous replication to the secondary region
options.B: Read access to secondary-region data without a failover
options.C: Write access to both regions at the same time
options.D: Zone redundancy in the primary region

content.explanation: By default, secondary data isn't readable until failover. RA- options let you read it anytime (it may lag due to RPO). Why not the others: A — Secondary replication is always asynchronous. · C — The secondary is read-only. · D — Zone redundancy is the 'Z' in GZRS, not the 'RA'.

content.question: Customer invoices are accessed infrequently and stored for at least 30 days. Which blob access tier fits best?

options.C: Archive
options.D: Hot

content.explanation: Minimum retention: Cool 30 days, Cold 90 days, Archive 180 days. The module uses invoices as its Cool example. Why not the others: B — For data stored at least 90 days. · C — For rarely accessed data stored at least 180 days, with flexible latency. · D — For frequently accessed data.

content.question: Which blob access tier can NOT be set as the default at the storage account level?

options.C: Hot
options.D: Cool

content.explanation: Hot, Cool, and Cold can be account defaults. Archive can only be set at the blob level. Why not the others: A — Can be set at the account level. · C — Can be set at the account level. · D — Can be set at the account level.

content.question: Which storage service is designed for reliable messaging between application components, with messages up to 64 KB?

options.C: Azure Queues
options.D: Azure Blobs

content.explanation: Queue Storage holds millions of messages for asynchronous processing and is often paired with Azure Functions. Why not the others: A — Managed SMB/NFS file shares. · B — NoSQL structured, non-relational data. · D — Unstructured object storage.

content.question: Which tool keeps an on-premises Windows Server and your Azure cloud shares in TWO-WAY sync, acting as a local cache with optional cloud tiering?

options.C: Azure Storage Explorer
options.D: AzCopy

content.explanation: File Sync turns a Windows server into a local cache of Azure Files, synced in both directions, with optional cloud tiering. Why not the others: A — A migration hub for workloads, not ongoing file sync. · C — A GUI for managing files and blobs; it uses AzCopy under the hood. · D — AzCopy sync is one-direction only.

content.question: Which tool does Azure Storage Explorer use on the back end to perform its file and blob tasks?

options.C: Azure Data Box
options.D: AzCopy

content.explanation: Storage Explorer is a GUI over AzCopy. Why not the others: A — A migration hub. · B — A separate sync service for Windows file servers. · C — A physical device for bulk offline transfer.

content.question: True or false? AzCopy synchronization is bi-directional, based on timestamps.
content.explanation: AzCopy sync is one-direction: you designate source and destination.

content.question: True or false? The Archive tier has the lowest storage cost but the highest access cost and rehydration latency.
content.explanation: Cheapest to store, most expensive and slowest to get back.

content.question: True or false? Replication to the secondary region is asynchronous, so a regional failure could cause some data loss.
content.explanation: The gap is the recovery point objective (RPO) — typically under 15 minutes, with no SLA.

content.question: True or false? NFS Azure file shares can be accessed from Windows clients.
content.explanation: NFS shares are accessible from Linux or macOS. SMB shares work with Windows, Linux, and macOS.

content.question: True or false? With GRS, data in the secondary region is readable at any time by default.
content.explanation: Secondary data isn't readable until failover unless you choose RA-GRS or RA-GZRS.

content.question: True or false? All data written to an Azure storage account is encrypted by the service.
content.explanation: Listed under the 'Secure' benefit of Azure Storage.

content.question: True or false? Azure Migrate is a physical device that is shipped to your datacenter.
content.explanation: That's Azure Data Box. Azure Migrate is an online hub for assessment and migration.

content.question: True or false? Data in Azure Storage is always replicated three times in the primary region.
content.explanation: Both LRS and ZRS keep three copies in the primary region.

content.question: Scenario: A healthcare company must (1) survive a full regional outage, (2) read its data from the secondary region during an outage without waiting for failover, and (3) stay available through a zone failure in the primary region. Which redundancy option fits?

options.C: RA-GRS
options.D: GZRS

content.explanation: GZRS covers zone failures (ZRS primary) and regional outages (geo-replication); the RA- prefix adds read access to the secondary. Why not the others: B — Meets 3 only — there's no secondary region. · C — Meets 1 and 2, but LRS in the primary doesn't survive a zone failure. · D — Meets 1 and 3, but you can't read the secondary without failover.

content.question: Scenario: A company must move a 70 TB on-premises archive to Azure once, over a slow internet link. Afterward, branch offices need fast local access to file shares that stay synced with Azure Files. Which combination fits?

options.A: Azure Migrate for the transfer, then Azure Storage Explorer for access
options.B: Azure Data Box for the transfer, then AzCopy sync
options.C: AzCopy for both the transfer and the ongoing sync
options.D: Azure Data Box for the bulk transfer, then Azure File Sync

content.explanation: Data Box handles large offline transfers when bandwidth is limited. File Sync provides local caches with bi-directional sync. Why not the others: A — Storage Explorer is a manual GUI, not a sync service. · B — AzCopy can't give branches a bi-directionally synced local cache. · C — Too slow for 70 TB here, and AzCopy sync is one-way with no local cache.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: Which service synchronizes user identities between on-premises Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID?

options.C: Microsoft Entra Connect
options.D: Microsoft Entra Conditional Access

content.explanation: Entra Connect bridges on-premises AD and Entra ID so users get one consistent identity (SSO, MFA, SSPR). Why not the others: A — Provides managed domain services (domain join, LDAP, Kerberos) — it isn't the AD-to-Entra sync tool. · B — Handles identities from outside your tenant. · D — Evaluates sign-in signals to allow/block/require MFA.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: A legacy app can't use modern authentication and needs LDAP, group policy, and Kerberos/NTLM in Azure, without you deploying or managing domain controllers. Which service fits?

options.C: Azure Key Vault
options.D: Microsoft Entra Connect

content.explanation: Domain Services provides a managed domain (Azure deploys and manages two DCs as a replica set) for apps that can't use modern auth. Why not the others: B — Adds a sign-in factor; doesn't provide domain services. · C — Stores secrets, keys, and certificates. · D — Syncs identities; it doesn't provide Kerberos/LDAP domain services.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: In multifactor authentication, a fingerprint scan belongs to which category?

options.C: Something the user has
options.D: Something the user knows

content.explanation: Know = password or question. Have = phone or code. Are = biometric. Why not the others: A — Not one of the three categories. · C — A phone receiving a code. · D — Passwords and challenge questions.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: Which is NOT one of the three passwordless options supported by Microsoft Entra ID?

options.C: One-time passcodes sent by SMS
options.D: Windows Hello for Business

content.explanation: The three passwordless options are Windows Hello for Business, the Microsoft Authenticator app, and FIDO2 security keys. Why not the others: A — This IS a passwordless option. · B — This IS a passwordless option. · D — This IS a passwordless option.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: Which passwordless option is an unphishable hardware device (USB, Bluetooth, or NFC) built on the WebAuthn standard?

options.A: A phone call from Microsoft Entra MFA
options.C: Microsoft Authenticator app
options.D: FIDO2 security keys

content.explanation: FIDO2 is an open standard; the hardware key handles authentication with no password to expose. Why not the others: A — An MFA method, not a passwordless hardware key. · B — Biometric/PIN tied to the user's own Windows PC. · C — Turns an iOS/Android phone into the sign-in factor.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: Which External ID capability gives external users access to Teams shared channels through a mutual trust, WITHOUT representing them in your directory?

options.C: Microsoft Entra Connect
options.D: External ID for customers

content.explanation: B2B direct connect = mutual two-way trust between Entra tenants, currently for Teams shared channels; users aren't in your directory. Why not the others: A — B2B collaboration users ARE represented in your directory, typically as guests. · C — Syncs on-premises AD with Entra ID. · D — For publishing apps to consumers, not partner Teams channels.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: Which sequence describes how Conditional Access works?

options.C: Physical → perimeter → data
options.D: Verify explicitly → least privilege → assume breach

content.explanation: It collects signals (user, location, device, app), decides, then enforces (allow, block, or require MFA). Why not the others: A — That's Microsoft Defender for Cloud's three needs. · C — Those are defense-in-depth layers. · D — Those are the Zero Trust principles.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: Azure RBAC is enforced on which actions?

options.A: Actions on Azure resources that go through Azure Resource Manager
options.B: Data-level access inside your own custom application's code and database
options.C: Only actions taken through the Azure portal interface
options.D: Only network traffic flowing to virtual machines

content.explanation: RBAC applies to anything through Resource Manager (portal, Cloud Shell, PowerShell, CLI). It does NOT enforce app- or data-level access. Why not the others: B — Application security must be handled by your app. · C — Also CLI, PowerShell, Cloud Shell — anything via Resource Manager. · D — Network filtering is NSGs, not RBAC.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: One role assignment grants you read access to a resource group and another grants write access to the same group. What's the result?

options.A: Write only, because the newest assignment wins
options.B: You have both read and write access
options.C: No access until the conflict is resolved
options.D: Read only, because the most restrictive assignment wins

content.explanation: Azure RBAC uses an allow model: permissions from multiple assignments add up. Why not the others: A — Assignment order doesn't matter. · C — Assignments don't conflict in an allow model. · D — RBAC is additive, not most-restrictive.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: Which is NOT a guiding principle of Zero Trust?

options.A: Assume breach and segment access to limit impact
options.B: Verify explicitly using all available data points
options.C: Trust devices that are on the internal corporate network
options.D: Use least privilege access with just-in-time and just-enough access

content.explanation: Zero Trust grants access based on authentication, not network location. The principles are verify explicitly, use least privilege, and assume breach. Why not the others: A — A Zero Trust principle. · B — A Zero Trust principle. · D — A Zero Trust principle.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: Which defense-in-depth layer uses DDoS protection to filter large-scale attacks before they cause a denial of service?

options.C: Perimeter
options.D: Application

content.explanation: Perimeter = DDoS protection and perimeter firewalls. Network = segmentation and deny-by-default between resources. Why not the others: A — Limits communication between resources (segmentation, deny by default). · B — Protects buildings and hardware in the datacenter. · D — Keeps apps secure and free of vulnerabilities.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: Microsoft Defender for Cloud fills which three needs?

options.A: Verify explicitly, least privilege, and assume breach
options.C: Identity, perimeter, and data
options.D: Continuously assess, secure, and defend

content.explanation: Assess = know your posture/vulnerabilities; Secure = harden with the Microsoft cloud security benchmark; Defend = alerts and threat protection. Why not the others: A — That's Zero Trust. · B — That's Conditional Access. · C — Those are defense-in-depth layers.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: To extend Defender for Cloud protection to on-premises machines, what do you deploy?

options.C: Microsoft Entra Connect
options.D: Azure Migrate

content.explanation: Deploy Azure Arc and enable Defender's enhanced security features to protect non-Azure servers. Why not the others: B — Private connectivity, not security onboarding. · C — Syncs identities; it doesn't onboard machines. · D — Moves workloads into Azure rather than protecting them in place.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: True or false? Permissions granted at a parent scope in Azure RBAC are inherited by child scopes.
content.explanation: Owner at a management group can manage everything in all of its subscriptions.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: True or false? In defense-in-depth, physical security is the outermost layer and data is at the center.
content.explanation: Physical → identity & access → perimeter → network → compute → application → data.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: True or false? Microsoft Defender for Cloud can only protect resources that run in Azure.
content.explanation: It also covers hybrid (via Azure Arc) and other clouds such as AWS and GCP.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: True or false? Zero Trust grants access based on network location rather than authentication.
content.explanation: The reverse — Zero Trust requires authentication and doesn't trust location.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: True or false? Conditional Access can skip MFA at a known location but require it when sign-in signals are unusual.
content.explanation: This is the 'more granular MFA experience' described in the module.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: True or false? Resources created directly in a Microsoft Entra Domain Services managed domain sync back to Microsoft Entra ID.
content.explanation: Sync is one-way: from Microsoft Entra ID to the managed domain.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: True or false? Azure RBAC enforces access at the application and data level inside your app.
content.explanation: RBAC covers Resource Manager actions; application security is your app's job.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: True or false? Single sign-on is only as secure as the initial authenticator.
content.explanation: Every later connection relies on that first authentication.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: True or false? Azure Key Vault is the primary Azure service for securely storing secrets, encryption keys, and certificates.
content.explanation: Centralizes secrets and keys instead of hard-coding them in apps.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: Scenario: Security wants to (1) require MFA for administrators, (2) block sign-ins from unexpected countries, and (3) allow access to the HR app only from compliant, managed devices. Which tool fits?

options.C: Defender for Cloud's secure score recommendations
options.D: Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies

content.explanation: All three are signal-based sign-in decisions — exactly Conditional Access's common scenarios. Why not the others: A — RBAC grants permissions on resources; it doesn't evaluate sign-in signals like location or device. · B — Azure Policy governs resource configuration, not user sign-ins. · C — Measures posture; it doesn't enforce sign-in conditions.

topic: Describe Azure identity, access, and security

content.question: Scenario: (1) A supplier's staff need to collaborate on internal apps using their own work accounts, with access reviewed periodically. (2) A public customer app must let people sign up with Google or Facebook accounts. Which combination fits?

options.A: B2B collaboration with access reviews; External ID for customers
options.B: Local accounts for each supplier; Entra Connect for the customer app
options.C: Entra Domain Services for suppliers; SSO for customers
options.D: B2B direct connect for both groups

content.explanation: B2B collaboration brings partners in as guests (with access reviews); External ID for customers handles consumer sign-up with social identities. Why not the others: B — Local accounts are what External ID avoids, and Entra Connect syncs on-prem AD. · C — Neither handles external or consumer identities. · D — Direct connect currently supports Teams shared channels only, not consumers.

content.question: Which of these is NOT one of the factors the module lists as affecting Azure costs?

options.A: Resource type and the settings you choose
options.B: The number of people who sign in to the Azure portal
options.C: Third-party solutions bought in Azure Marketplace
options.D: The geography (Azure region) where your resources are deployed

content.explanation: Listed factors: resource type, consumption, maintenance, geography, subscription type, and Azure Marketplace. Why not the others: A — A listed factor. · C — A listed factor — you may also pay the third-party vendor. · D — A listed factor — prices and data transfer vary by region.

content.question: How is data transfer (bandwidth) generally priced in Azure?

options.A: Some inbound transfers are free; outbound transfers are priced by billing zone
options.B: Outbound transfers are free; inbound transfers are charged
options.C: All data transfer is free within the same geography
options.D: Inbound and outbound data transfers are always charged at one identical flat rate

content.explanation: Data going INTO Azure is often free; data LEAVING Azure is priced based on zones. Why not the others: B — Reversed. · C — Not stated — outbound pricing depends on zones. · D — Inbound and outbound are treated differently.

content.question: What is the difference between a billing zone and an availability zone?

options.A: A billing zone is an availability zone located inside a paid region
options.B: They're two names for the same physical datacenter concept
options.C: Billing zones group regions for pricing; AZs are datacenters
options.D: A billing zone is another name for a pair of Azure regions

content.explanation: Same word, different concepts. Billing zones exist only for pricing; availability zones are physical isolation. Why not the others: A — Billing zones are groups of regions, not datacenters. · B — They're explicitly different. · D — Region pairs are for resiliency, not pricing.

content.question: Which statement about the Azure Pricing Calculator is TRUE?

options.A: It produces your exact final invoice in advance
options.B: It still includes the TCO calculator for comparing against on-premises costs
options.C: It provisions a trial version of the resources you select
options.D: It only estimates costs; nothing is provisioned and you aren't charged

content.explanation: The calculator is for information only. Also note: the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculator has been RETIRED. Why not the others: A — It's an estimate only. · B — The TCO calculator has been retired — an older-material trap. · C — Nothing is provisioned.

content.question: Which is NOT one of the three types of alerts shown in Cost Management's cost alerts?

options.C: Department spending quota alerts
options.D: Budget alerts

content.explanation: The three cost alert types are budget alerts, credit alerts, and department spending quota alerts. Resource Health belongs to Azure Service Health. Why not the others: B — A cost alert type (EA prepayment). · C — A cost alert type (EA customers). · D — A cost alert type.

content.question: When are credit alerts generated?

options.A: At any threshold you configure in the portal
options.B: At 50% and 75% of the credit balance
options.C: Only once the credit balance reaches 100%
options.D: Automatically at 90% and 100% of the credit balance

content.explanation: Credit alerts track Azure Prepayment for Enterprise Agreements and fire automatically at 90% and 100%. Why not the others: A — Credit alert thresholds are fixed. · B — Those percentages are examples of department spending quota thresholds. · C — They also fire at 90%.

content.question: Which service can require new resources to have an Owner tag, and can reapply tags that were removed?

options.C: Azure Policy
options.D: Cost Management budgets

content.explanation: Azure Policy enforces tagging rules and conventions, including requiring and reapplying tags. Why not the others: A — Prevent deletion or changes; they don't add tags. · B — Gives recommendations; it doesn't enforce rules. · D — Track spend; they don't enforce tags.

content.question: Which option has you commit to an hourly SPEND amount on eligible compute for 1 or 3 years, with flexibility across compute types?

options.C: Reserved capacity (Azure Reservations)
options.D: Azure Spot Virtual Machine pricing

content.explanation: Savings plan = commit to spend, flexible across compute. Reservations = commit to specific resources. Spot = unused capacity that can be evicted. Why not the others: A — No commitment and no discount. · C — Commit to specific resource capacity, not a flexible spend amount. · D — No commitment; discounted capacity that Azure can reclaim.

content.question: True or false? Department spending quota alerts are specific to Enterprise Agreement customers.
content.explanation: They notify department owners when spending reaches a fixed threshold of the quota.

content.question: True or false? Deprovisioning a VM always automatically removes its associated storage and networking resources.
content.explanation: Those resources may not be deprovisioned at the same time — that's why maintenance is a cost factor.

content.question: True or false? The same VM configuration can cost different amounts in different regions.
content.explanation: Power, labor, taxes, and fees vary by location.

content.question: True or false? Reservations can apply to services such as VMs, databases, and storage, for one- or three-year terms.
content.explanation: Listed in the consumption factor and the cost optimization unit.

content.question: True or false? Microsoft sets the billing structure for third-party solutions bought through Azure Marketplace.
content.explanation: Billing structures are set by the vendor.

content.question: True or false? Resources automatically inherit tags from their resource group.
