content.explanation: Resources don't inherit tags from subscriptions or resource groups. Use Azure Policy if you need tags applied consistently.

content.question: Scenario: Match each workload to the best pricing option. (1) A production SQL workload running 24/7 with stable needs. (2) Batch rendering jobs that can restart if interrupted. (3) A web/API workload with steady total usage that shifts among compute services.

options.A: (1) Azure savings plan for compute, (2) Spot pricing, (3) Reservations
options.B: (1) Spot pricing, (2) Reservations, (3) Azure savings plan for compute
options.C: (1) Reservations, (2) Azure savings plan for compute, (3) Spot pricing
options.D: (1) Reservations, (2) Spot pricing, (3) Azure savings plan for compute

content.explanation: This matches the module's decision guide exactly: stable/predictable → Reservations; interruptible → Spot; steady but flexible → savings plan. Why not the others: A — Reservations lock you to specific resources — bad for a workload that shifts across services. · B — Spot for 24/7 production risks eviction; Reservations add no value for restartable batch jobs. · C — Spot for steady web/API traffic risks evictions, and batch is the ideal Spot candidate.

content.question: Scenario: A dev/test subscription keeps overspending. The team wants a notification at 80% of a monthly budget, automatic shutdown of nonproduction resources when the threshold is hit, and a view of costs by resource group. What should they use?

options.A: Credit alerts, which fire at 90% and 100% of the balance
options.B: Azure Advisor cost recommendations reviewed every week
options.C: A Cost Management budget with an 80% alert, automation, and cost analysis
options.D: A Pricing Calculator estimate, plus resource locks on the whole subscription

content.explanation: Budgets set limits and alerts and can trigger automation; cost analysis shows costs by subscription, resource group, or service. Why not the others: A — Credit alerts are for EA prepayment balances and use fixed thresholds. · B — Advisor suggests savings but doesn't alert at a budget threshold or automate shutdown. · D — Estimates don't monitor live spend, and locks don't shut anything down.

content.question: What are the two main solution areas of Microsoft Purview?

options.A: Risk and compliance, and unified data governance
options.C: Azure Policy definitions and resource locks
options.D: Threat assessment and active threat defense

content.explanation: Purview is a family of data governance, risk, and compliance solutions. Why not the others: B — That's Microsoft Entra ID. · C — Those are Azure governance features, not Purview's areas. · D — Sounds like Defender for Cloud.

topic: Describe features and tools in Azure for governance and compliance

content.question: Where can Microsoft Purview's unified data governance manage data?

options.A: Microsoft 365 services such as Teams only
options.B: On-premises, multicloud (e.g., Amazon S3), and SaaS
options.C: On-premises SQL Server databases only
options.D: Azure subscriptions only, not other clouds

content.explanation: Purview brings insights about on-premises, multicloud, and SaaS data together — not just Azure. Why not the others: A — Microsoft 365 is a core part of risk and compliance, but governance reaches further. · C — Too narrow. · D — Too narrow — Purview spans other clouds too.

topic: Describe features and tools in Azure for governance and compliance

content.question: What is an Azure Policy initiative?

options.A: A lock that prevents resources from being deleted
options.B: A role assignment that grants permissions at a scope
options.C: A group of related policy definitions toward a larger goal
options.D: A JSON template that deploys resources

content.explanation: Initiatives bundle policies, e.g., 'Enable Monitoring in Azure Security Center' contains 100+ definitions. Why not the others: A — That's a resource lock. · B — That's Azure RBAC. · D — That's an ARM template.

topic: Describe features and tools in Azure for governance and compliance

content.question: What does a ReadOnly resource lock do?

options.A: Authorized users can read the resource but can't update or delete it
options.B: Users can't read the resource at all
options.C: It applies only to users who aren't owners
options.D: Authorized users can read and modify the resource but can't delete it

content.explanation: ReadOnly is similar to restricting everyone to the Reader role's permissions. A Delete lock still allows reads and modifications. Why not the others: B — ReadOnly allows reading. · C — Locks apply regardless of RBAC role — even owners. · D — That's a Delete lock.

topic: Describe features and tools in Azure for governance and compliance

content.question: You're an Owner of a resource that has a Delete lock, and you need to delete it. What must you do?

options.A: Assign yourself the Contributor role, then delete it
options.B: Remove the lock first, then delete the resource
options.C: Nothing — Owners automatically bypass resource locks
options.D: Open a support ticket, since locks can't be removed

content.explanation: Locks apply regardless of RBAC permissions. Modifying a locked resource is a two-step process. Why not the others: A — No RBAC role overrides a lock. · C — Even owners must remove the lock first. · D — Locks can be removed by anyone with permission to manage them.

topic: Describe features and tools in Azure for governance and compliance

content.question: What is the Microsoft Service Trust Portal used for?

options.A: Enforcing configuration rules and standards on your Azure resources
options.B: Classifying sensitive data across your estate
options.C: Tracking outages that affect your Azure services
options.D: Reading Microsoft's security, privacy, and compliance reports

content.explanation: It provides content about how Microsoft implements controls that protect its cloud services and customer data. Why not the others: A — That's Azure Policy. · B — That's Microsoft Purview. · C — That's Azure Service Health.

topic: Describe features and tools in Azure for governance and compliance

content.question: You create a policy that allows only certain VM sizes. What happens to VMs that existed before the policy?

options.A: They're ignored; only new VMs are evaluated
options.B: Azure Policy evaluates them and flags any noncompliant VMs
options.C: They're automatically exempt from all policies
options.D: They're deleted automatically

content.explanation: Azure Policy evaluates all current resources, including ones created before the policy, and highlights noncompliance. Why not the others: A — Existing VMs are evaluated too. · C — Exemptions are something you mark explicitly. · D — Policy doesn't delete existing resources.

topic: Describe features and tools in Azure for governance and compliance

content.question: True or false? Resource locks apply regardless of RBAC permissions.
content.explanation: Even an Owner must remove the lock before performing the blocked action.

topic: Describe features and tools in Azure for governance and compliance

content.question: True or false? A Delete lock prevents authorized users from modifying a resource.
content.explanation: A Delete lock still allows reads and modifications; only deletion is blocked. ReadOnly blocks modifications.

content.question: True or false? A resource lock on a resource group doesn't affect the resources inside it.
content.explanation: Locks are inherited — a lock on a resource group applies to every resource in it.

topic: Describe features and tools in Azure for governance and compliance

content.question: True or false? Azure Policy can automatically remediate some noncompliant resources, such as adding a missing tag.

content.question: True or false? Some Service Trust Portal resources require signing in with a Microsoft cloud services account and accepting an NDA.

topic: Describe features and tools in Azure for governance and compliance

content.question: True or false? Azure Policy can only report noncompliance; it can't prevent noncompliant resources from being created.
content.explanation: Azure Policy can prevent noncompliant resources from being created.

topic: Describe features and tools in Azure for governance and compliance

content.question: Scenario: (1) All resources must be deployed only to EU regions. (2) A production database must not be deleted accidentally, even by admins. (3) Auditors want Microsoft's independent audit reports. Which combination fits?

options.A: (1) Azure Policy, (2) RBAC Reader role, (3) Service Trust Portal

options.C: (1) Microsoft Purview, (2) Delete lock, (3) Azure Advisor
options.D: (1) Azure Policy, (2) Delete lock, (3) Service Trust Portal

content.explanation: Policy enforces allowed locations; a Delete lock blocks deletion regardless of role; the Service Trust Portal hosts Microsoft's compliance documents. Why not the others: A — RBAC doesn't stop admins (owners) from deleting; a lock does. · B — Locks don't restrict location; Purview governs YOUR data, not Microsoft's audit reports. · C — Purview doesn't enforce deployment locations; Advisor doesn't provide audit reports.

topic: Describe features and tools in Azure for governance and compliance

content.question: Scenario: A data team needs an up-to-date map of all its data across Azure SQL, on-premises databases, and Amazon S3, including sensitive data classification and end-to-end lineage. Which service fits?

options.C: Microsoft Purview
options.D: Microsoft Defender for Cloud

content.explanation: Data map, classification, and lineage across on-premises, multicloud, and SaaS is Purview's unified data governance. topic: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

content.question: Which statement describes Azure Cloud Shell?

options.A: A desktop app you install locally that supports PowerShell only
options.B: A shell that requires a separate sign-in using a service principal account
options.C: A GUI dashboard that replaces the Azure portal
options.D: A browser-based, pre-authenticated shell for PowerShell or Azure CLI

content.explanation: No local install, it knows who you are and your permissions, and you choose PowerShell or Bash (CLI). Why not the others: A — It's browser-based and supports both. · B — It's authenticated with your Azure credentials. · C — It's a command-line shell inside the portal.

topic: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

content.question: What is the PRIMARY difference between Azure PowerShell and the Azure CLI?

options.A: The Azure CLI is graphical, PowerShell is text-based
options.B: Syntax: the CLI uses Bash-style commands; PowerShell uses cmdlets
options.C: Azure PowerShell can't be installed on Linux or macOS
options.D: The Azure CLI can only handle one-off tasks, not repeatable automation

content.explanation: They're functionally equivalent; the choice mostly comes down to which language you know. Why not the others: A — Both are command-line tools. · C — Both install on Windows, Linux, and Mac. · D — Both can orchestrate complex operations through scripts.

topic: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

content.question: Which service receives every request from the portal, CLI, PowerShell, APIs, and SDKs, then authenticates and authorizes it?

options.C: Azure Cloud Shell
options.D: Microsoft Entra Connect

content.explanation: Resource Manager is Azure's deployment and management layer — every tool goes through the same API, so results are consistent. Why not the others: B — Extends management to non-Azure resources; it isn't the request-handling layer. · C — One of the tools that sends requests to Resource Manager. · D — Syncs on-premises identities.

topic: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

content.question: How do ARM templates define what to deploy?

options.A: As a YAML pipeline that runs in Azure DevOps
options.B: As imperative PowerShell commands executed step by step
options.C: In declarative JSON that describes the desired end state
options.D: As Bash scripts that run inside Cloud Shell

content.explanation: You define WHAT you want; Resource Manager handles HOW (ordering, dependencies, parallel deployment). Why not the others: A — Not the ARM template format. · B — That's scripting, not a declarative template. · D — Templates CAN call scripts, but the template itself is declarative JSON.

topic: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

content.question: What is Bicep?

options.A: A declarative language that deploys through ARM, simpler than JSON
options.B: An imperative scripting language that replaces the Azure CLI and PowerShell
options.C: A query language for Azure Monitor logs
options.D: A deployment engine that bypasses Resource Manager

content.explanation: Bicep is an easier-to-read alternative to JSON ARM templates; deployments still go through Resource Manager. Why not the others: B — Bicep is declarative and doesn't replace the CLI. · C — That's the query language used in Log Analytics. · D — Bicep deploys THROUGH Resource Manager.

topic: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

content.question: How does Azure Arc let you manage resources outside Azure?

options.A: By creating a private network circuit to Azure
options.B: By replicating resources to the paired region
options.C: By migrating on-premises servers into Azure VMs
options.D: By projecting non-Azure resources into Resource Manager

content.explanation: Arc makes servers, Kubernetes clusters, SQL Server, and more appear in Resource Manager so you can use Azure governance and monitoring on them. Why not the others: A — That's ExpressRoute. · B — That's geo-redundancy, not Arc. · C — That's Azure Migrate.

topic: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

content.question: Why is the Azure portal resilient to individual datacenter failures?

options.A: It goes offline during scheduled maintenance windows
options.B: It runs in every Azure datacenter and updates without downtime
options.C: It's hosted in a single primary region with a standby
options.D: It's accessible only through Cloud Shell during outages

content.explanation: That also keeps it close to users, which avoids network slowdowns. Why not the others: A — It updates continuously with no downtime. · C — It's present in every datacenter. · D — Cloud Shell is accessed through the portal, not the other way around.

topic: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

content.question: True or false? Copilot in Azure recommendations can be applied straight to production without review because they come from Azure.
content.explanation: Treat Copilot as an assistant — validate recommendations, confirm permissions, and review changes first.

topic: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

content.question: True or false? You must install the Azure CLI locally before you can use Azure Cloud Shell.
content.explanation: Cloud Shell is browser-based and requires no local installation.

topic: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

content.question: True or false? Azure Arc can manage Kubernetes clusters and SQL Server instances that run outside Azure.
content.explanation: Arc supports servers, Kubernetes clusters, Azure data services, SQL Server, and VMs (preview).

topic: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

content.question: True or false? With ARM templates, Resource Manager handles dependency order and parallel deployment.
content.explanation: Orchestration is one of the listed template benefits.

topic: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

content.question: True or false? Infrastructure as code means configuring each resource manually in the portal and documenting the steps.
content.explanation: IaC manages infrastructure through code and templates instead of manual configuration.

topic: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

content.question: True or false? Because RBAC is built into Azure Resource Manager, you can apply access control to all services.
content.explanation: Listed as a Resource Manager benefit.

topic: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

content.question: Scenario: A team must deploy identical dev, test, and prod environments repeatedly, in a consistent state, with dependencies deployed in the right order, using syntax that's easy to read. What should they use?

options.B: Manual configuration in the Azure portal for each environment
options.C: Bicep files deployed through Azure Resource Manager
options.D: Commands typed by hand into Cloud Shell each time

content.explanation: Bicep gives declarative, repeatable (idempotent) deployments with built-in orchestration and simpler syntax than JSON. Why not the others: A — Manages non-Azure resources; it isn't a deployment template. · B — Not repeatable or consistent. · D — Not declarative or reliably repeatable.

topic: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

content.question: Scenario: An organization runs servers on-premises and Kubernetes clusters in another public cloud. It wants to apply the same Azure Policy rules and keep one inventory, managed from Azure. What should it use?

options.C: ARM templates
options.D: Azure Arc

content.explanation: Arc extends Azure governance, policy, and inventory to hybrid and multicloud resources from one place. Why not the others: A — Moves workloads into Azure; doesn't manage them where they are. · B — Provides connectivity, not governance. · C — Deploy Azure resources; don't bring outside resources under Azure management.

content.question: Which is NOT one of Azure Advisor's five recommendation categories?

options.C: Reliability
options.D: Cost

content.explanation: The five categories are Reliability, Security, Performance, Operational Excellence, and Cost. Why not the others: B — An Advisor category. · C — An Advisor category. · D — An Advisor category.

content.question: Which Service Health view gives a global picture of Azure health across ALL services and regions?

options.C: Azure Advisor
options.D: Service Health

content.explanation: Azure Status = global. Service Health = the services and regions YOU use. Resource Health = an individual resource. Why not the others: B — Scoped to an individual resource. · C — Gives recommendations, not health status. · D — Scoped to the services and regions you use.

content.question: Which tool tells you whether a SPECIFIC virtual machine is healthy, and whether a problem is on Azure's side or yours?

options.C: Resource Health
options.D: Azure Status

content.explanation: Resource Health zooms in on individual resources. Why not the others: A — Recommendations, not health status. · B — Services and regions you use, not a single resource. · D — Global view only.

content.question: What is Log Analytics used for?

options.A: Writing and running queries against data that Azure Monitor collects
options.C: Sending synthetic requests to check that your app is still responding
options.D: Notifying you about Azure outages in your regions

content.explanation: Log Analytics is where you query logs, from simple filters to advanced trend analysis. Why not the others: B — That's Azure Advisor. · C — That's Application Insights availability tests. · D — That's Service Health.

content.question: What two components make up an Azure Monitor alert setup?

options.A: A signal plus an enforcement action at sign-in time
options.B: A budget and a spending threshold percentage
options.C: An alert rule (condition) and an action group (response)
options.D: A policy initiative and a policy definition

content.explanation: The rule defines the condition; the action group defines the response. Why not the others: A — That's Conditional Access language. · B — That's Cost Management. · D — That's Azure Policy.

content.question: Action groups can be reused across which services?

options.A: Azure Monitor and Cost Management only
options.B: Azure Monitor, Service Health, and Azure Advisor
options.C: Azure Monitor only
options.D: Defender for Cloud and Azure Policy only

content.explanation: The module states action groups are reusable across all three. Why not the others: A — Not what the module lists. · C — They're reusable beyond Monitor. · D — Not what the module lists.

content.question: What does Application Insights monitor?

options.A: Only web apps hosted in Azure App Service
options.C: Azure platform outages and planned maintenance in your regions
options.D: Performance and usage of web apps, wherever they run

content.question: True or false? Azure Advisor recommendations must be acted on immediately; they can't be postponed or dismissed.
content.explanation: Each recommendation can be acted on right away, postponed, or dismissed.

content.question: True or false? Service Health shows outages, planned maintenance, and health advisories for the services and regions you use.
content.explanation: Because you're signed in, it knows which services matter to you, and you can set alerts.

content.question: True or false? A metric alert can email you when a VM's CPU stays above 80%.
content.explanation: The module's own metric alert example.

content.question: True or false? Azure Monitor works only with Azure resources.
content.explanation: Azure Monitor works with Azure, on-premises, and multicloud environments.

content.question: True or false? Resource Health gives a global view of Azure health across all regions.
content.explanation: That's Azure Status. Resource Health covers individual resources.

content.question: True or false? Application Insights can be enabled without code changes by using an agent.
content.explanation: You can add the SDK OR enable the agent without code changes.

content.question: Scenario: A web app is intermittently slow. The team wants to (1) know when response times and failure rates spike, and (2) confirm the app is still responding overnight, when real traffic is near zero. What should they use?

options.A: Resource Health for the app's VM
options.C: Azure Advisor performance recommendations
options.D: Application Insights, including availability tests

content.explanation: Application Insights tracks response times and failure rates; availability tests send synthetic requests even during low traffic. Why not the others: A — Shows whether the VM is healthy, not app response times. · B — Shows global Azure health, not your app's behavior. · C — Suggestions, not real-time app telemetry or uptime checks.

content.question: Scenario: You hear about a major cloud outage in the news. You want to (1) find out if it affects the services and regions you use, with alerts for future events, and (2) check whether your specific VM is affected. Which combination fits?

options.A: Azure Advisor alerts, plus Service Health alerts
options.B: Service Health with alerts, plus Resource Health for the VM
options.C: Log Analytics queries, plus Application Insights
options.D: The Azure Status page, plus Azure Advisor alerts

content.explanation: Service Health covers your services/regions (with alerts); Resource Health covers the individual VM. Why not the others: A — Advisor doesn't check the health of a specific VM. · C — Your own telemetry won't tell you about Azure platform incidents. · D — Azure Status isn't personalized and has no alerts; Advisor doesn't report outages.
